> The model is identified, yet I get the following error messages:

I disagree -- this model is not identified because the TiP construct is undefined.  I'm unfamiliar with the particular article you cited, but if you review either of the attached articles that discuss formative "measurement," you'll see that a formative construct is only "identified" if it is predicting at least one endogenous observed variable or latent construct that is locally identified in its own right.

I use the quotation marks because I have a hard time considering this to be a measurement model at all.  I can't argue with psychometricians like MacCallum and Bollen, who are infinitely smarter than I am and have written on the topic of formative measurement, but I can't shake the impression that the prospect of formative measurement is illusory.  If you are familiar with phantom constructs, you might notice that the only situations in which a formative construct is identified is when it can be interpreted as a phantom construct for whatever dependent variable(s) it predicts.  If there are multiple DVs it predicts, you can also interpret it as a latent construct (reflectively) defined by those DVs, which is being predicted by the IVs you think of as formative indicators.

It wouldn't be appropriate to start a discussion about formative measurement on this blog, but similar to the need to consider alternative equivalent models, I wanted to point out alternative interpretations of the same model you are trying to fit (if you find a way to identify the TiP construct).

Terry

messages.body_plain:
The LMRR and MR approaches provide the F values but the Mplus approach provide the chi-square value. Mplus uses the asymptotic property of the F distribution such that, if the denominator df is large, the F distribution multiplied by the numerator df is convergent to the chi-square distribution with the df equal to the numerator df of the F distribution. You will see that the F value of the MR approach multiplied by 10 (degree of freedom) is the Mplus chi-square value.

Sunthud

messages.body_plain:
Hi Robin

When you are using ordered variables, intercepts are not estimated, what is estimated instead are thresholds. So, for example if a variable have 3 categories it will have 2 thresholds.

The syntax for thresholds would be:

var | t1 ## indicating the first threshold for the variable var

If you are using the "group.equal" argument in the cfa function you can add "thresholds" instead of intercepts. If you are doing it by syntax you can do the next:

var1 | c(th1,th1)*t1
var1 | c(th2,th2)*t2

var2 | c(th3,th3)*t1
var2 | c(th4,th4)*t1

this will constraint the 2 thresholds for variables var1 and var2 equal across 2 groups.

hope it helps

 -Mauricio

messages.subject: Re: Unidentified model
messages.body_plain:
It is possible that the model is just a really bad fit for a constrained factor model, offering no best set of parameter estimates that conforms to rules such as "residual variances must be positive."  One can create a covariance matrix that forces residual variances to be negative without inducing an identification problem.  Look at the parameter estimates that lavaan can provide--see if they are headed off into extreme parameter space.  Also, try looking at the *correlation* matrix only for this group to see if proportionality constraints appear to hold, and if plausible loading values would make sense.
     Also, if there is an identification problem here, it is an empirical identification problem, meaing that it is a problem with the sample data, not the structure of the model per se.  With n = 200 divided into 3 groups, the membership in Group 1 may be fairly small, so that the algorithm does not detect some effects as significant because of low n, leading in turn to an identification problem.
     Remember that, with an iterative estimation procedure, empirical identification is a matter of the parameter estimates right now, on this iteration.  Sometimes estimation runs temporarily through bad parameter space, but it could come out into good estimates if it had the chance.  You could try to avoid the bad parameter space by setting starting values that are "different from zero" and on the same side of zero where you expect the final estimates to fall.
--Ed Rigdon

Did you fix all the factor loadings? By default, coef() will only return
the 'free' parameters in your model. You can get all parameters

coef(fit, type="all")

parameterEstimates(fit)$est

Or if you ONLY want the factor loadings, something like

PE <- parameterEstimates(fit)
PE[ PE$op == "=~", "est"]

Yves.

messages.subject: Re: Unidentified model
messages.body_plain:
Josef--
     A chapter by Karl Joreskog, "Basic Ideas in Factor and Component Analysis" first explained this to me.
     If two observed variables A and B are both congeneric indicators of the same single common factor, then the ratio of their correlations with any third variable C must be a constant ratio or proportion across all other C in the model, at the population level.  So at the population level is must be true that:
corr(A,C) / corr(B,C) is a constant across all C.
    So you can look at a correlation matrix and determine whether a given factor model seems to hold, without estimating a model.  You can at least see gross violations of these proportionality constraints.  Your n is low, so there will be a lot of random sampling error obscuring the correlations, but you might be able to visually detect the kind of major reversal of proportionality, such as (for any two other variables C and D):
corr(A,C) > corr(B,C) but  corr(A,D) < corr(B,D)
which would signal a major fit problem.
     So what I was asking was whether the correlation matrix looked like the factor model ought to hold.  If you saw a major problem, that could explain a failure to converge normally, even if the moel isn technically identified.
--Ed Rigdon

I'm guessing you have time-series data, running a p-technique type of analysis, since you are investigating fit for different individuals...  Regardless, if the problem is that there is no beta matrix in the null model, you can add one in a way that should not affect the fit or degrees of freedom for the null model.

Generate a vector of random numbers (normal, uniform, whatever), and regress that vector on all the variables in your model.  Save the residuals in another vector, which is then a vector of random numbers that are completely orthogonal to all variables in the model (correlations = 0).  You could also do this in a single step:

myData$ranOrth <- resid(lm(rnorm(nrow(myData)) ~ myData$var1 + myData$var2 + ... + myData$varN))

Since ranOrth is uncorrelated with any variable, you can run the null model as before, but additionally fix the correlations of all other variables with ranOrth to zero, except for one.  For one of the original model variables, specify instead that the regression path to ranOrth is zero.  I haven't tried it yet, but that should introduce the beta matrix into the model, allowing you to view MIs, but without changing the degrees of freedom or the (lack of) fit, since the observed associations are actually null to begin with.  But check those values, because I may not be thinking of everything.  Oh, and if you are analyzing the covariance matrix and mean vector instead of raw data, it is easy to simply use cbind() and rbind() to add a row/column of zeros corresponding to another orthogonal variable, specifying a nonzero variance for it.

Terry

HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3

               textual ~~ speed

On 09/13/2013 03:22 PM, robin ghertner wrote:

> indicators. As Rene, I'm following the Vandenberg framework for
> configural->strict invariance. The problem I'm running into is
> constraining the residual variances, using group.equal="residuals". When
> I do so, the model doesn't change at all - all fit indices are identical
> to the configural model (i.e. no constraints).

The 'delta' parameterization currently used by lavaan when data are
categorical does not estimate the residuals (they are a function of
other model parameters). Hence, group.equal="residuals" has not effect.
(Perhaps a warning would be in order).

But you can constrain the 'delta' scaling factors to be equal across
groups, although you will have to do it manually. There is no
group.equal argument for it now.

If x1, x2, x3, ... are indicators of a latent variable, you could write
something like:

x1 ~*~ c(d1,d1,d1)*x1
x2 ~*~ c(d2,d2,d2)*x2
x2 ~*~ c(d3,d3,d3)*x2
...

In this example, I have assumed three groups. By setting the labels
equal across groups, the delta factors will be constrained to be equal.

Yves.

This is just a different definition. Interestingly, Mplus 4.1 or older
would have reported 0.125. But newer versions report 0.328.

You can 'switch' between the two versions as follows:

lavaan:::standardize.est.all(fit.cfa.Store_traits2)

[15] 0.1864880 0.3351869 0.2657427 0.2885129 0.3152068 0.1681252 0.1992799
[22] 0.2460296 0.2233733 0.2420121 0.4318303 1.0000000 1.0000000 1.0000000
[29] 1.0000000 0.7939579 0.4726158 0.6647278 0.5117308 0.4986659 0.4987489

# for the 0.125 version
  lavaan:::standardize.est.all(fit.cfa.Store_traits2, cov.std=FALSE)
  [1] 0.8574204 0.9019490 0.8153607 0.8568882 0.8434969 0.8275223 0.9120717
  [8] 0.8948297 0.8683147 0.8812643 0.8706250 0.7537703 0.1249241 0.2648303
[15] 0.1864880 0.3351869 0.2657427 0.2885129 0.3152068 0.1681252 0.1992799
[22] 0.2460296 0.2233733 0.2420121 0.4318303 1.0000000 1.0000000 1.0000000
[29] 1.0000000 0.7939579 0.4726158 0.6647278 0.5117308 0.4986659 0.4987489

In the 'old' tradition, off-diagonal residual covariances were computed
by the formula cov(i,j) / sqrt(i.var*j.var) where i.var and j.var are
diagonal elements of OV. In the 'new' tradition, the i.var and j.var
elements are the 'THETA' diagonal elements, as Terry said. The latter
has the advantage that it gives you the correlation between the two
residuals.

I do agree with Ivo that it is a bit illogical that the variances are
not '1', but 1-R^2. We 'assume' this is what the applied users really
want to see ;-)

Yves.

Given a simple non-sense model

HS.model <- ' test  =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + x5'

there are 10 free parameters to estimate: 4 factor loadings, 1 factor variance, 5 indicator variances. Since we have p = 5 indicators there are p(p+1)/2 = 15 information elements in the variance-covariance-matrix. The model is overidentified, df = 15-10 = 5.
When I fit the model with

fit.ml <http://fit.ml> <- cfa(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939)

summary(fit.ml <http://fit.ml>, fit.measures = TRUE)

parTable(fit.ml <http://fit.ml>)

the output shows exactly what I mentioned above: df = 5, free parameters = 10.

When I fit the model using MLR estimator with

fit.mlr <- cfa(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939,  estimator="MLR")

summary(fit.mlr, fit.measures = TRUE)

parTable(fit.mlr)

 the intercepts are also estimated which means an increase of free parameters of 5, so 15 all together. But the summary still shows df = 5.

So my questions are:

1) Why does the MLR estimator automatically estimate the item intercepts?
2) Why does this increase in free parameters not lead to a decrease in degrees of freedom?

Thanks a lot,

model. The lavaan approach is to ignore the data as long as possible: we
parse your model syntax, figure out what is observed and what is latent,

lavNames( parTable(fit), type="ov" )

for the sample data is

inspect(fit, "sampstat")

which will use the same order as fitted().

But wait a minute. lavaan 0.5-14 is actually right! df should be 7, not
10. And it should be df=7 both for fixed.x=TRUE and fixed.x=FALSE.

The 'bug' is not in lavaan 0.5-14, but in 0.5-13 (and possibly in

lavaanNames(fit, type="ov.x", group=1)

did not correctly return the list of exogenous variables (in 0.5-13 and
before). This has been corrected in 0.5-14, and as a happy coincidence
also cured the (latent) df bug for the baseline model when we have
exogenous variables and fixed.x=FALSE.

So why is df=7 (and not 10). Because 3 out of the 5 variables are
exogenous. And under the baseline/independence model, we only assume
that all endogenous variables are uncorrelated; we DO allow for
correlations among the exogenous variables.

Yves.

uhmmm... i see. well, now i'm finding this to be a very, very interesting situation. quoting from EQS 6's pdf manual, page #117 under the Independence Model heading:

"The chi-square associated with the model of independent or uncorrelated variables is presented first".

by quickly inspecting the EQS outputs (even the ones in the manual) it's relatively straightforward to verify that the formula to calculate the degrees of freedom for this model is: number of unique elements in the covariance matrix - the number of elements in the diagonal. so, for the example above, that's 10 dfs because EQS' assumes that the independence/baseline model is a diagonal matrix.

HOWEVER...

after re-fitting the same model in Mplus i can see that Mplus reports 7 dfs! just as lavaan 0.5-14! so, in this case, the fomula would be the number of unique elements in the covariance matrix - number of elements elements in the diagonal - the number of covariances among exogenous variables.

which, therefore, suggests there are actually two different viewpoints of what constitutes an independence/baseline model, Peter Bentler's and Bengt Muthen's.

lavaan 0.5-14 didn't have a bug then. it's just using a different definition of what the baseline/independence model is.

thanks for pointing that out... makes me wonder what other theoretical distinctions exist between the EQS way of doing things and the Mplus way.

> "drive" is the rate parameter of a Poisson process that governs the
> random variable "degree". Further I want to fit a regression model where
> this latent drive variable predicts consistent condom use (logit link

I'm afraid not. lavaan (0.5-14) only supports normally distributed
latent variables; and has only support for continuous, binary or ordered
observed variables, using a probit link function.

It would seem you need a custom programmed routine for this. I would
hunt down a local SAS/R guru for this.

Yves.

There are many, many differences. I often mention this in presentations
(see eg http://users.ugent.be/~yrosseel/lavaan/lavaan_IMPS_2013.pdf).

One of the aims of the lavaan project is to 'mimic' all these
differences (well, as many as possible).

In dev 0.5-15, using mimic="EQS" in your example will result in df=10
for the baseline model.

>      If two observed variables A and B are both congeneric indicators of the same single common factor, then the ratio of their correlations with any third variable C must be a constant ratio or proportion across all other C in the model, at the population level.  So at the population level is must be true that:
> corr(A,C) / corr(B,C) is a constant across all C.
>     So you can look at a correlation matrix and determine whether a given factor model seems to hold, without estimating a model.  You can at least see gross violations of these proportionality constraints.  Your n is low, so there will be a lot of random sampling error obscuring the correlations, but you might be able to visually detect the kind of major reversal of proportionality, such as (for any two other variables C and D):
> corr(A,C) > corr(B,C) but  corr(A,D) < corr(B,D)
> which would signal a major fit problem.

On 09/24/2013 09:28 AM, Martin Ogonowski wrote:
> Dear all,
>
> I am quite new to SEM and I would like to specify some residual
> covariances in my model which I can do using the  double tilde notation.
> What I do not understand is why I get estimates for all possible
> correlations in the summary output even though I did not specify them.
> Do I have to supress these unwanted correlations in the syntax or what
> is it that I have failed to understand?

The following covariances are automatically added to the model (if you
are using the sem() function):

- covariances between exogenous latent variables (lv.x)
- covariances between endogenous observed variables (ov.y)

To find out what lavaan considers to be lv.x or ov.y, type:

lavNames(fit, type="lv.x")
lavNames(fit, type="ov.y")

If you really must suppress these, you can either add fix them to zero
in the syntax, eg

light ~~ 0*antro

or you can use the lavaan() function, where you need to add all your
parameters yourself (perhaps using the auto.* arguments)

Yves.

Hi Peter,

The first warning indicates that your sample covariance matrix can't be inverted.  This has nothing to do with the fitted model, so you can look for problems in the sample covariance a couple of ways.  You could use the cov2cor() function to standardize the covariance matrix, and look for any out-of-bounds values or indications of redundancy between two variables.  But it might be a case of multicollinearity (i.e., one variable is redundant with a linear combination of 2 or more other variables), which you probably wouldn't be able to notice in a correlation matrix.  In your case, it turns out that the 2 categorical variables are completely redundant with each other: c2 = -(c1 - 1), so they are perfectly negatively correlated:

So you only need one of those to define your H construct.  (By the way, in the path diagram, the factor loadings need to point in the other direction; i.e., latent factors predict observe variables, not the other way around). > det(cov(dat[ , -1]))
[1] 7.402503e-08

sem(model, data, ordered = c("c2", "x4", "x5"))

messages.subject: Re: shared variance
messages.body_plain:
You mean the covariance (or correlation) matrix among latent constructs?  If you are running a CFA, then that is simply the PSI matrix:

inspect(output, "coef")$psi
cov2cor(inspect(output, "coef")$psi)

If you have structural regressions (in the BETA matrix), then PSI is the residual covariance matrix.  In that case, the total covariance matrix is a function of BETA and PSI, but you can get it this way:

inspect(output, "cor.lv <http://cor.lv>")

There's a list of information you can get with inspect() under the Methods section of the lavaan-class help page:

?lavaan::inspect

Terry
